questions.question_text: A physiotherapist records only each patient's grip strength during a check-up. Is this univariate or bivariate data?

options.text: Univariate — only one variable, grip strength, is recorded for each patient.
Bivariate — because grip strength is measured in two hands.
options.why: Treats two measurements of the same characteristic as two different variables.

options.text: Bivariate — because many patients are involved.
options.why: Confuses the number of individuals surveyed with the number of variables recorded.

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the patients' ages.
options.why: Assumes an unrecorded characteristic affects the classification, which depends only on what is actually recorded.

questions.solution_text:
Only one characteristic, grip strength, is recorded for each patient.
One variable means the data is **univariate**.

questions.question_text: A car dealership records each car's engine size and its fuel efficiency (km per litre), to see whether the two are related. Name the two variables in this bivariate dataset.

options.text: Engine size and fuel efficiency.
Car and fuel efficiency.
options.why: Names the individual (the car) instead of the characteristic recorded about it.

options.text: Engine size and the dealership.
options.why: Names the place the data was collected rather than the second measured characteristic.

options.text: Fuel efficiency only.
options.why: Names only one characteristic, but bivariate data must involve two variables.

questions.solution_text:
The two characteristics being recorded are engine size and fuel efficiency.
The variables are **engine size** and **fuel efficiency**.

questions.question_text: Countries that eat more chocolate per person tend to have more Nobel Prize winners per person. Does eating more chocolate cause more Nobel Prizes to be won?

options.text: No — this is likely a coincidental or confounded correlation, not a proven causal link.
Yes — the strong correlation proves chocolate causes higher intelligence.
options.why: Treats a strong correlation as proof of causation, which it never is on its own.

options.text: No — because the two variables are not bivariate data.
options.why: Misapplies the univariate/bivariate classification to a question about causation instead.

options.text: Yes — chocolate must be the cause because it was recorded first in the data.
options.why: Assumes the order variables are listed or recorded in determines which one is the cause.

questions.solution_text:
A correlation between two national averages does not show that one causes the other.
Wealthier countries can afford more chocolate and tend to invest more in research, so national wealth is a more believable explanation for both.
No — this is likely a coincidental or confounded correlation, not a proven causal link.

questions.question_text: A study compares people's favourite colour with their blood type across a large sample, finding every blood type occurs about equally often for every favourite colour. Is there an association between favourite colour and blood type?

options.text: No — there is no association; the blood types are spread evenly across every colour.
Yes — because both are categorical variables, they must be related.
options.why: Assumes the type of variable (categorical) determines whether an association exists.

options.text: Cannot say — an association can only be found for numerical variables.
options.why: Wrongly restricts the concept of association to numerical variables only.

options.text: Yes — a large sample size always produces an association.
options.why: Confuses a large sample size with evidence of a relationship between the variables.

questions.solution_text:
An association would need one colour to occur more or less often at particular blood types.
Here every blood type is spread evenly across every favourite colour.
No — there is no association between favourite colour and blood type.

questions.question_text: In coastal towns, the number of surf lifesaving club members and the number of sunscreen bottles sold both increase in summer. A student claims joining a surf club causes people to buy more sunscreen. Identify the real explanation.

options.text: Both are driven by a confounding variable — warmer summer weather brings more people to the beach, increasing both club membership and sunscreen sales.
The claim is correct, since both increase at the same time.
options.why: Treats two variables rising together as proof that one causes the other.

options.text: Sunscreen sales cause more people to join surf clubs.
options.why: Reverses the claimed direction of causation without recognising that neither variable causes the other.

options.text: The two variables cannot be compared because they are measured in different units.
options.why: Raises an irrelevant objection about units instead of addressing whether the correlation is causal.

questions.solution_text:
Both variables rise in summer, but neither directly causes the other.
Warmer weather is the confounding variable — it brings more people to the beach, which increases both club membership and sunscreen sales.
The real explanation is a confounding variable, not a causal link between the two.

questions.question_text: A survey records both a person's number of siblings and their favourite season, to see whether the two are linked. Is this univariate or bivariate data?

options.text: Bivariate — two variables, number of siblings and favourite season, are recorded for the same people.
Univariate — because favourite season is not a number.
options.why: Assumes a variable must be numeric to count towards the classification.

options.text: Univariate — because there is no clear cause and effect between them.
options.why: Confuses the univariate/bivariate classification with whether a causal relationship exists.

options.text: Cannot say without knowing how many people were surveyed.
options.why: Assumes sample size affects the classification, which depends only on how many variables are recorded.

questions.solution_text:
Two characteristics — number of siblings and favourite season — are recorded for the same people.
Two variables recorded on the same individuals means the data is **bivariate**.
